full-fine-tuning.d: Fine-tuning in which all of the model’s parameters receive a gradient and optimizer state. With AdamW in mixed precision it costs ~16 bytes of state per parameter, not counting activations.

precisao-mista.d: Training with the forward and backward in BF16/FP16 (or FP8 in the GEMMs) while the update additions happen on an FP32 copy of the weights (the master weights). It combines the speed of low precision with the accuracy of high precision.

pesos-mestres.d: FP32 copy of the weights kept by the optimizer in mixed precision. The step is added to it (23 mantissa bits) and only the copy used in the forward is rounded to BF16, so that updates smaller than half a BF16 ulp are not lost. Costs 4 B/parameter.

estado-do-otimizador.d: Everything training keeps per parameter besides the weight: the gradient, the optimizer buffers (AdamW’s moments \(m\) and \(v\), Muon’s momentum) and, in mixed precision, the FP32 master weight. It scales with the number of trainable parameters, not with the text.

bytes-por-parametro.d: The unit of training memory math. BF16 inference: 2. Full FT with mixed-precision AdamW: 16 (2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4). Mixed-precision Muon: 12. Pure BF16 + AdamW: 8. 8-bit AdamW or BF16 Muon: ~6. LoRA: 2 (or ~0.52 in NF4) per frozen parameter and ~16 per adapter parameter.

soma-de-kahan.d: A technique that keeps aside the remainder lost when rounding each addition and gives it back in the next addition. It lets you accumulate many small increments in a format with a short mantissa (such as BF16) without losing them.

arredondamento-estocastico.d: Rounds up or down with probability proportional to the distance to each representable neighbor, so that the expected value is exact. It lets steps smaller than half an ulp accumulate on average in BF16 optimizers.

memoria-de-ativacoes.d: Intermediate tensors saved during the forward because the backward needs them. In a Transformer with FlashAttention, ≈ \(34\,s\,b\,h\) bytes per layer (Korthikanti et al.): it grows with sequence length and microbatch size, not with the number of parameters.

gradient-checkpointing.d: Saves only the input of each layer (\(2sbh\) bytes) and recomputes the rest in the backward. It trades memory for compute: activations drop from \(34sbhL\) to ≈ \(2sbhL + 34sbh\), and the cost rises from ~6N to ~8N FLOPs per token.

clipping-de-gradiente.d: Rescales the gradient vector when its norm exceeds a limit (max_grad_norm, typically 1.0), so that a bad batch does not take a giant step.

adamw-8bit.d: A variant of AdamW (bitsandbytes) that stores the moments \(m\) and \(v\) quantized to 8 bits in blocks, with one scale per block. It reduces optimizer state from 8 to ~2 B/parameter; quality should be measured.

adafactor.d: An optimizer that, instead of storing a matrix’s full second moment \(v\), stores only the row and column means and reconstructs it as an outer product. State memory becomes sublinear in the size of the matrix.

warmup-de-lr.d: Initial phase in which the learning rate rises gradually from ~0 to the peak, to avoid large steps while the optimizer’s statistics are still raw. Expressed as a fraction of the steps (0.03; 0.1) or in steps/tokens.

schedule-cosseno.d: Learning-rate decay along half a cosine cycle, from the peak down to a final value (often 0), usually after a warmup. The default in Axolotl, LLaMA-Factory, and MiMo’s SFT.

wsd.d: A three-phase learning-rate schedule: warmup, a long constant plateau, and a final decay. MiMo-V2-Flash pretraining: warmup to 3.2e-4 over 50 B tokens, constant for 12T, and cosine down to 1e-4 over 10T.

lote-efetivo.d: Examples (or tokens) per optimizer step: microbatch × gradient accumulation steps × data-parallel replicas. It is the quantity that published hyperparameters assume.

acumulacao-de-gradiente.d: Summing the gradients of several microbatches before one optimizer step. It increases the effective batch without increasing activation memory and amortizes the (bandwidth) cost of the optimizer step.

packing.d: Putting several short examples together in the same max_length row so positions are not spent on padding. In TRL: bfd (best-fit decreasing, the default), bfd_split, and wrapped; with padding_free and variable-length FlashAttention, one example does not attend to another.

zero-dp.d: A family of data-parallel techniques that partitions the training state across the \(N_d\) processes instead of replicating it: ZeRO-1 splits the optimizer, ZeRO-2 also the gradients, ZeRO-3 also the parameters (≈ FSDP FULL_SHARD), at the cost of 1.5× the communication.

fsdp.d: PyTorch’s native implementation of ZeRO-3: each process keeps a shard of weights, gradients, and state, and gathers (all-gather) each layer’s parameters only when it is about to use them. FSDP2 (fully_shard) shards per parameter on top of DTensor.

context-parallel.d: Parallelism that splits the sequence across ranks (ring attention, Ulysses) to train with very long context; each rank keeps the activations of one piece of the text.

lora.d: Fine-tuning that freezes \(W_0\) and learns only a low-rank correction: \(h = W_0x + \frac{\alpha}{r}BAx\), with \(A\in\mathbb R^{r\times d_{in}}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{d_{out}\times r}\), and \(B = 0\) at the start. It trains \(r(d_{in}+d_{out})\) numbers per matrix and can be merged afterward.

escala-alfa-lora.d: The factor that multiplies the correction \(BA\). With the \(1/r\) prefactor, the optimal LR barely changes with the rank. Conventions: a fixed α = 32, α = 2r, r16/α32. In mlx-lm, scale is already the whole factor (scale 20 ≡ α/r = 20).

rslora.d: A LoRA variant that uses the scale \(\alpha/\sqrt r\) instead of \(\alpha/r\), to stabilize high ranks (use_rslora=True in PEFT).

peft.d: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: methods that train a small fraction of the parameters (LoRA, DoRA, adapters…), and also the name of the Hugging Face library that implements them (LoraConfig, merge_and_unload).

qlora.d: LoRA on top of a base frozen in 4 bits: NF4 with double quantization (4.127 bits/param), adapters in 16/32 bits, and paged optimizers. The paper fine-tuned a 65B model on a 48 GB GPU; a 70B fits on a DGX Spark.

nf4.d: QLoRA’s 4-bit format with 16 levels at the quantiles of a standard normal normalized to [−1, 1] (8 positive, 7 negative, and an exact zero) and an absmax scale per block of 64 weights. Well suited to Gaussian weights; dequantized to BF16 before the GEMM.

quantizacao-dupla.d: Quantizing the quantization scales themselves: in QLoRA, the FP32 scales of the 64-weight blocks become 8 bits in blocks of 256. The cost of the scales drops from 0.5 to 0.127 bit/param (4.127 bits in total).

otimizador-paginado.d: An optimizer whose state lives in NVIDIA unified memory and is paged between GPU and CPU at usage peaks, to avoid OOM. On a machine with physically unified memory (GB10, Apple Silicon) it creates no new capacity.

loftq.d: An initialization of \(A\) and \(B\) that compensates for the base’s quantization error in a QLoRA (init_lora_weights="loftq" in PEFT).

dora.d: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation: \(W' = m\cdot\frac{W_0 + BA}{\lVert W_0 + BA\rVert_c}\). A trainable vector \(m\) handles the magnitude of each column and LoRA handles only the direction. It closes part of the gap to full FT and is also mergeable.

lora-plus.d: A variant that gives \(B\) a larger learning rate than \(A\) (ratio λ ≈ 16, loraplus_lr_ratio).

lora-por-expert.d: In an MoE, one pair of adapters for each expert, stored as 3D tensors \([E, r, d_{in}]\) and \([E, d_{out}, r]\) and indexed by the routing. Thinking Machines convention: rank per expert = total rank ÷ active experts. The router stays frozen.

merge-de-adaptador.d: Adding the learned correction into the weights: \(W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA\). After that, the inference cost is zero. In a QLoRA, the adapter was correcting \(\mathrm{deq}(W_{NF4})\), so measure the KLD after merging and requantizing.

multi-lora.d: Serving several LoRA adapters on top of the same base, chosen per request. In vLLM: --enable-lora, --lora-modules, --max-loras, and --max-lora-rank; the prefix caching hash includes the LoRA ID.

mfu.d: The fraction of the hardware’s peak FLOP/s that training actually uses, counting only the model’s FLOPs (≈ 6N per token in full FT). Used to estimate time: \(t = \text{tokens}\cdot kN/(\text{MFU}\cdot F)\).
